deal_summary: A leasing-mediated equipment purchase moved from an internally reviewed proposal through contract edits and a signed scan into shipment and acceptance planning; dispatch and acceptance arrangements were still being coordinated at the last visible exchange (evidence: 0-10).

customer_need.summary: The customer needed equipment configured for specified packaging and label dimensions, with the leasing documentation identifying the intended equipment and use (evidence: 1-2).

deal_dynamics.early: The leasing-side contact said the case was partly prepared from prior supplier work, had been passed internally, and might reach signing soon (evidence: 0).
deal_dynamics.middle: Packaging specifications, compliance documents, and significant legal edits were exchanged; the leasing side sent a revised contract for review (evidence: 1-4).
deal_dynamics.late: A signed contract scan arrived and the customer asked about shipment timing; urgent delivery and who could sign acceptance then became unresolved coordination topics (evidence: 5-10).

positive_signals: The leasing contact reported internal circulation and sent a signed contract scan (evidence: 0,5).
The customer requested shipment timing and proposed alternatives for delivery and acceptance (evidence: 6-8,10).
customer_behavior.initiative: Customer and leasing contacts proactively requested compliance documentation, asked when shipment could be planned, and proposed a different acceptance location after the initial authorization route was rejected (evidence: 2,6,8,10).
customer_behavior.decision_process: Contract review involved leasing legal staff and higher-level approval; delivery and acceptance depended on coordination among the customer, leasing recipient, vendor legal team, and production (evidence: 3-5,8-10).

strong_actions: Raised the need to attach packaging and label specifications to the contract and engaged on legal and acceptance questions (evidence: 1,9-10).
manager_behavior.follow_up_quality: Contract comments and the later authorization question received follow-up, but the production response on dispatch timing was still pending in the last visible exchanges (evidence: 4,9-10).
manager_behavior.next_step_control: Contract documentation advanced; confirming an acceptable delivery and acceptance route and obtaining a production date remained open (evidence: 5-10).

turning_points.description: The leasing contact sent a scan of the signed purchase contract and immediately asked when shipment could be planned.

The leasing contact said the customer could issue a power of attorney for acceptance, but vendor legal declined to act as signer; the leasing contact then proposed acceptance at the leasing recipient.

primary_trajectory_explanation.explanation: The visible trajectory moved from contract and compliance review to a signed scan, then shifted to shipment scheduling and the permitted acceptance route. The view ends with the alternative route being checked, so it does not establish that dispatch or acceptance was completed (evidence: 3-10).

secondary_factors: A leasing intermediary and its legal review shaped the documentation and acceptance process (evidence: 2-5,8-10).
The initial contact described prior work with another supplier and said the opportunity was partly prepared before this sequence (evidence: 0).

limits: Vendor legal rejected the proposed power-of-attorney arrangement, and production had not yet confirmed shipment timing in the last visible call (evidence: 9-10).
The view does not show whether the alternate acceptance route was approved or whether a different follow-up would have changed the timeline.

evidence.paraphrase: Leasing-side contact said the opportunity was partly prepared from prior supplier work, had been sent for internal analysis, and might reach signing the following week.
The call covered attaching the end-customer container and label specifications to the contract and clarifying the parties involved in the leasing purchase.
Leasing requested a conformity certificate, declaration, or equipment passport.
Leasing said material contract changes required higher-level review and that it expected a decision that day.
Leasing sent a contract with legal comments and accepted edits for review and agreement.
Leasing sent a scan of the signed purchase contract.
The end-customer contact asked when shipment could be planned.
The customer requested delivery by Wednesday and asked whether the vendor could arrange a carrier at the customer's expense.
Leasing said the customer would be absent from Moscow and was ready to issue a power of attorney for acceptance, asking if a vendor employee could sign.
Vendor legal declined the power-of-attorney plan because the vendor was an interested party; production had not yet confirmed the shipping date.
Leasing proposed shipment to its recipient, with the acceptance act signed there, and asked the vendor to confirm the route.
